summary: Reviews examples of limited domains, also called controlled environments, where network behaviors and semantics are specific to a restricted region of the internet. Policies, options, management and security may differ from the open internet.

plainLanguage.summary: A limited domain is a network region with its own technical rules. This RFC describes why such regions exist and what a protocol must explain if it works only within one.

questions: can internet protocols behave differently inside a controlled network
what is a controlled environment in networking
why do some internet protocols only work inside one network
what are the requirements for limited domain membership
how can a limited domain be defined
subtitle: How protocols and policies can be limited to a defined part of the Internet.

tldr.problem: Networks have different technical requirements, but Internet protocols often assume they must work across the whole Internet. Middleboxes and local policies can make that assumption fail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys limited-domain examples, classifies four ways a protocol can behave across domain boundaries, and lists functions needed to establish domain membership securely.
tldr.outcome: It proposes no protocol. It argues that a limited-domain protocol should say which boundary scenario applies and how the domain is defined, while preserving the open Internet as the general method of interconnection.

today: RFC 8799 is an Informational Independent Submission published in July 2020. It is not an Internet Standards Track specification, and the RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: What Counts as a Limited Domain
sections.content:
A limited domain is a network or network region with requirements, behavior, or meanings that differ from the wider Internet. It can be a physical place, such as a building or vehicle, or a group of users connected through a virtual network.

The term does not mean a DNS naming domain. The RFC uses controlled environment for the same general idea and focuses on technical requirements, not on political or language-based restrictions to information flow.
sections.plainLanguage: A limited domain is a network region with technical rules that apply there. It may be a physical network or a virtual group spread across different places.

sections.title: Why Internet Paths Can Fail
sections.content:
The RFC says the Internet has no well-defined mechanism for identifying limited domains. As a result, middleboxes can block protocol features, and network mechanisms such as IPv6 extension headers, Path MTU Discovery, and IP fragmentation may fail on some paths.

Administrative boundaries can also leak traffic when router rules are misconfigured. Requiring a node to be explicitly configured for a limited-domain protocol can reduce that risk, but limited use does not remove the need for sound design and security.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls and other middleboxes may block traffic they do not recognize. A network operator can also misconfigure a boundary and let traffic cross it by mistake.

sections.title: Domains and Their Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC surveys domains ranging from homes, vehicles, sensor networks, and enterprises to data centers, content delivery networks, and large service-provider networks. Their requirements can differ in performance, management, security, privacy, and connectivity.

It also describes tools whose meanings are limited by a network, including locally significant Differentiated Services Code Points, service-function chains, segment routing, and deterministic networking. These examples may still benefit from interoperable specifications, even when they are not meant to operate across the whole Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks need different capabilities. Examples include home networks, vehicle networks, data centers, and systems that require predictable delivery times.

sections.title: Four Boundary Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four scenarios. In A, a protocol follows normal IP formats and can cross the Internet between parts of a domain. In B, it does not follow those formats and cannot cross the Internet directly. In C, the protocol is declared invalid outside its originating domain, so a boundary must block it or a tunnel must create one virtual domain.

In D, separate domains assign different meanings to the same protocol values, so combining them can cause unpredictable results. A protocol specification should identify its scenario and explain the domain boundary; the RFC does not recommend abandoning globally interoperable standards.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol can cross a domain boundary, fail there, or be required to stop there. If different domains give its values different meanings, joining those domains can cause problems.

sections.title: Membership and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says domain membership should be managed with minimal manual setup and cryptographic protection. It lists a unique verifiable domain identity, nesting and overlap, node eligibility, secure enrollment and withdrawal, optional temporary membership, verifiable roles, peer checks, and access to domain policy.

A boundary may also be a trust boundary. Operators need a way to identify interior and boundary nodes, protect operational information, and use credentials tied to the domain. Whether packets need a domain marker or their own cryptographic authentication is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: A system needs a reliable way to identify a domain, admit or remove members, and check their roles. The RFC lists these needs but does not design a membership protocol.
